title: Shimano reveals new SPD-SLR pedal system with lower stack height and new shoes to match
content:
Cyclist
Shimano reveals new SPD-SLR pedal system with lower stack height and new shoes to match

Shimano has officially launched its new SPD-SLR pedal system. Alongside updated Dura-Ace and Ultegra pedals and new cleats, there are new top spec S-Phyre and mid-spec RC8 shoes to match. The SPD-SLR pedals and cleats are not compatible with the older SPD-SL system.

Shimano cites a lower stack height, faster engagement, lighter parts and easier adjustment as the benefits of the new system, which is the first major overhaul of Shimano’s road bike pedal system since SPD-SL was launched back in 2003.

The brand says that every contact point in the foot/shoe/pedal system has been re-engineered to increase stability and efficiency by reducing unnecessary movement. The result, Shimano says, ‘is a more direct connection between rider and bike, allowing power to flow more naturally while maintaining the comfort and reliability riders expect from Shimano’.

The new system lowers stack height by 2.3mm. ‘Old’ Dura-Ace SPD-SL PD-R9100 had a 14.6mm stack height, so this represents a reduction of almost 16%. Shimano says that the lower stack height results in a more stable pedalling platform, improved power transfer and improved control of the bike. 

It also claims that clipping in is easier with the new system, thanks to a wider catch zone for the cleat’s front retainer and an engagement angle of 10.5°, versus 15.5° for SPD-SL.

The new Shimano cleat design 

The SPD-SLR cleats may look superficially similar to SPD-SL and have the same coloured tongue and rear supports, but weight of the cleat-plus-bolts has been reduced from 71g to 55g, principally by removing the rectangular washers that SPD-SL needed between the cleat and the bolts.

There are new markings on the cleats to help you to get the alignment set up more easily too.

As with the SPD-SL cleats, there are yellow, blue and red cleats available with different amounts of float, +/-3o, 1o and 0o respectively. 

In addition, there’s a new grey cleat that is designed for compatibility with older SPD-SL shoes and offers the same +/-3o float as the yellow cleats. Although this doesn’t provide the reduced stack height of the other cleats, it does increase lateral adjustment range when used with SPD-SL shoes with fixed position bolt holes rather than a floating cleat plate.

SPD-SLR has been used by pros for a few months already, not least when Mathieu van der Poel was unable to ride Jasper Philipsen’s bike at Paris-Roubaix, following a puncture in the Trouée d’Arenberg, due to his SPD-SL cleats being incompatible with Philipsen’s SPD-SLR pedals. 

With the official launch, Shimano has confirmed the lack of cleat-to-pedal cross-compatibility between the two systems, although you can mount the SPD-SLR cleats to SPD-SL spec shoes.

New Shimano Dura-Ace and Ultegra pedals

Shimano pedals hadn’t seen any significant change in their design in years, but the new Dura-Ace PD-R9300 pedals drop the stack height, although they look superficially similar to the older model.

As with the PD-R9100, there are steel contact surfaces on the carbon composite pedal body and the inboard bearing is positioned to the side of the pedal platform, rather than under it, as in lower spec Shimano pedals. Shimano claims this increases stiffness by 11% relative to its new Ultegra pedals. Dura-Ace’s axle and bearings are stated to reduce friction by 53% relative to Ultegra.

Ultegra spec pedals too have seen an update to the new SPD-SLR system, with the new PD-R8200 pedals retaining the SPD-SL equivalent’s carbon shell.

New S-Phyre SH-RC910 shoes

To go with the new pedal system, Shimano has launched updated S-Phyre shoes, which it says offer more cleat adjustability, along with a carbon fibre heel cup that’s claimed to increase foot stability and its Dynalast 2.0 fit, that it says reduces foot fatigue.

A new upper design with a closer wrap around the foot and more ventilation and a new midsole that offers ventilation and water drainage are also claimed to improve fit and pedalling efficiency.  

Again, there’s a lower spec, less pricey alternative, the SH-RC810 shoes, which share much of the spec of the S-Phyre shoes, including two Boa Li2 dial closures, while adding replaceable heel pads to increase longevity.
